extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of logic and philosophy (readers of a logic textbook)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative principles for analyzing propositions, definitions, attributes, and syllogistic forms in categorical (Aristotelian) logic; includes criteria for what counts as informative propositions, correct definitions, and legitimate syllogistic transformations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclude metaphysical Noumena from Logic
rubrics_metrics.description: Metaphysical disputes (e.g., the reality of Noumena or Things-in-themselves) are irrelevant to Logic and should be avoided in a treatise of Logic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a doctrine (such as denial or affirmation of Noumena) does not affect the form of language or the essential doctrines of Logic it should not be introduced; introducing it only creates confusion. Logical theory should remain neutral on such metaphysical questions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of attributes (Bain's formulation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Attributes defined as 'points of community among classes.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This captures one point of view but is limited: it applies mainly to attributes of classes and is not ultimate, since the 'points of community' themselves admit further analysis (e.g., into resemblances in sensations). Be wary of treating this as exhaustive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of Total and Partial vs Universal and Particular (Bain)
rubrics_metrics.description: Propositions may be classified as Total and Partial (Bain) as opposed to Universal and Particular, reserving 'Universal/Particular' for their inductive sense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This nomenclature can advantageously group Singular propositions with Universal under 'Total predications' because what matters in reasoning is whether the assertion is about the whole or a part of what the subject denotes. However, traditional terms are familiar and the double meaning may cause little practical inconvenience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reading some universals as specialized predicates (quâ)
rubrics_metrics.description: A proposition may be considered equivalent to a universal with a modified predicate, e.g. 'All wine is good quâ wine' (i.e., good in respect of qualities which constitute it wine).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This helps interpret predicate scope and avoid equivocation about what the predicate is meant to convey in context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Knowledge vs Instinct distinction for tool-use claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Human use of instruments (e.g., using a spade) requires knowledge of the instrument and the object on which it is used, whereas animal instinctive actions may not presuppose the same kind of mental apprehension.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When asserting that an agent 'uses' or 'knows' an object, ensure the assertion is appropriate to human intentional knowledge, not illegitimately anthropomorphizing instinctive behavior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat classes as indefinite for logical purposes
rubrics_metrics.description: For Logic, classes should generally be considered indefinite (unenumerated) rather than definite (a fixed enumeration of individuals).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Definite classes (e.g., 'the Peers of the Realm') are often useless for pure logical purposes; indefinite classes allow the general rules of predication and inference to operate. Use definite classes only as abridged expression when useful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification of tacit errors in cognition
rubrics_metrics.description: Errors of perception and silent cogitation arise by passing from one imagination to another, feigning past or future events, false inferences from signs, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize these as common sources of fallacy; logic should account for and guard against mistakes coming from imagination, misleading signs, or unwarranted temporal inferences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction and relation between extension and intension
rubrics_metrics.description: Subject is naturally construed in its extension (the extent of class denoted) and predicate in its intension (connotation), but the extension is apprehended only through attributes (intension).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In analyzing propositions, do not treat extension and intension as independent primitives: the class extension is grasped via the attributes connoted by the term. This affects how one traces meaning and avoids certain equivocations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Existence as a separate predicate (Mill's view vs Bain)
rubrics_metrics.description: Existence can be predicated apart from causation or co-existence: the abstract name Existence and the connotation of Being consist in the capacity to excite some sensations or states of consciousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reject the view that 'existence' is merely elliptical or reducible to coexistence/causation. When discussing existence philosophically or logically, treat it as a distinct predicate whose meaning hinges on capacity to produce consciousness, and where questions of existence often depend on prior questions of causation or co-existence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Law of Relativity (Bain) and its limits
rubrics_metrics.description: The Law of Relativity: nothing can be perceived or apprehended except by contrast; Bain uses this to deny a summum genus 'Being'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accept that contrast is important for apprehension, but acknowledge that the necessary antithesis for consciousness may be 'nonentity' (nothing) rather than another positive fact; don't overread Bain's law to the point of denying the usefulness of abstract names like Being.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpret general names as knowledge/belief rather than 'idea of' (Smart's remark on Locke)
rubrics_metrics.description: Replace Locke's phrase 'the Idea of' with 'the knowledge of' to better capture what a name or proposition expresses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When explicating the import of propositions and names, prefer formulations that foreground belief/knowledge about the thing rather than the more ambiguous 'idea' terminology; this yields clearer analysis of propositional content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use Kant's analytic/synthetic distinction to classify judgments
rubrics_metrics.description: Analytic judgments can be evolved from the meaning of the terms; synthetic judgments add content beyond mere term-meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing whether a proposition conveys new information, determine whether the predicate is contained in the subject's connotation (analytic) or adds content (synthetic). This helps distinguish verbal from informative propositions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attributes do not form genera/species in same sense as things
rubrics_metrics.description: Although attributes may be put into classes, those classes can only be admitted to be genera or species 'by courtesy' because the distinction of kinds does not apply directly to attributes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid treating attributes' classes as full biological-style genera/species when doing classificatory work in logic; recognize the categorical difference between attributes and objects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition as 'sum of all properties connoted' (Bain) and its critique
rubrics_metrics.description: Bain's doctrine: a full definition is the sum of all properties connoted by the name (final, underivable properties); Mill objects that this would make many empirical truths into mere verbal truths and conflates specialist scientific connotations with common meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging a definition, distinguish ordinary/common connotation from specialized scientific connotation. A good general definition should reflect the properties connoted in ordinary use, not every discovered scientific property. Beware of calling empirically discovered facts 'mere verbal propositions' simply because specialists conjoin them with the name.

rubrics_metrics.name: Real vs Nominal/Descriptive definitions (Whately and De Morgan views)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whately: a Real Definition 'explains anything more of the nature of the thing than is implied in the name' (often a Description); De Morgan: a Real Definition may contain less than the Nominal Definition provided it suffices for distinction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be explicit which sense of 'real definition' is intended: philosophical (Whately) vs pragmatic (De Morgan). For purposes of distinction use De Morgan's criterion; for explaining deeper nature, follow Whately's descriptive expectation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish definitional premises from factual premises in syllogisms
rubrics_metrics.description: A premise that is merely definitional (part of the meaning of a term) does not function as a factual premise in establishing empirical conclusions; confusing definitional statements with factual assertions leads to fallacious inferences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating a syllogism, check whether a premise is a definition or an empirical claim. If it is definitional, the 'inference' may be merely verbal/equivalent transformation, not real reasoning about facts. Example: using 'A dragon is a thing which breathes flame' as a factual premise is illegitimate unless one means 'imagined as breathing flame.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Equivalent propositional forms (Obversion and other immediate inferences)
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain changes of expression (e.g., denying the negative) yield equivalent propositional forms; Bain designates obversion for denying the negative or vice versa.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use obversion, conversion and other equivalence transformations correctly as immediate inferences, but be cautious about hidden shifts in meaning when applying them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nonstandard conversion forms (e.g., 'Some A is not B' → 'No B is some A')
rubrics_metrics.description: Some propositions admit less familiar conversions, e.g., Sir W. Hamilton's observation that 'Some A is not B' may be converted to 'No B is some A' in certain readings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize and check such conversions for sense and applicability; they may be formally valid but can be misleading in ordinary language unless qualified.

rubrics_metrics.name: Categorize oppositions correctly: contraries/subcontraries/contradictories/subaltern relations
rubrics_metrics.description: Logical oppositions among categorical propositions should be classified: Contraries (All A is B / No A is B), Subtraries (Some A is B / Some A is not B), Contradictories (All A is B / Some A is not B; No A is B / Some A is B), with subalternate relations linking universals to particulars.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this taxonomy to test consistency and inferential relations among propositions; misclassifying oppositions can generate apparent paradoxes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of Singular Propositions in syllogistic reasoning
rubrics_metrics.description: Debate on whether singular propositions (e.g., 'Socrates is wise') should be classed with Universal (Total) propositions for ratiocination or treated differently; Bain argues to exclude them from syllogism while others include them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating a syllogism containing singulars, determine whether predicates are parts of the proper name's meaning (in which case inference may be mere repetition) or independent empirical claims (in which case genuine inference is possible). Avoid treating singulars as purely verbal if premises convey real information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Functional roles of syllogistic figures (Lambert/Bailey summary)
rubrics_metrics.description: Each syllogistic figure serves different epistemic purposes: first figure suits discovery/proof of properties of a thing; second for distinctions between things; third for instances and exceptions; fourth for discovery/exclusion of species of a genus.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose syllogistic figure appropriate to the inferential aim (property-discovery vs distinction vs exemplification). Be aware critics may dispute mapping to dictum de omni et nullo and propose alternate canonical axioms for each figure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Usefulness limits of De Morgan's numerically-definite syllogisms
rubrics_metrics.description: De Morgan's formalism derives definite conclusions from proportionally quantified premises (e.g., if 60% and 70% overlaps exist then at least 30% overlap).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although mathematically valid, such numerically-definite forms are rarely useful in ordinary reasoning because common premises lack numerical precision. Use them when genuine numerical proportions are known; otherwise they do not help guard against typical language-based fallacies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quantification of the predicate (Sir W. Hamilton) and its epistemic critique
rubrics_metrics.description: Hamilton's doctrine: take into account quantity of predicate as well as subject (e.g., 'All A is some B'). He claims many technical advantages (simpler conversion, unified laws, elimination of special syllogistic laws, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hamiltonian quantification can be used as an artificial test of syllogistic form since ordinary propositions can be recast to quantify predicates. However, Mill's critique: the quantification is not 'present in thought' and thus misrepresents the actual mental content of ordinary assertions; use it cautiously and be explicit about its artificiality.

rubrics_metrics.name: General names denote resemblances of sensations (Mill-Spencer debate)
rubrics_metrics.description: General names ultimately denote outward or inward phenomena consisting of feelings (resemblances of sensations); the attribute is the similarity itself, not a numerically identical entity across individuals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In conceptual analysis prefer treating general terms as standing for resemblances rather than multiple distinct attributes per individual; this preserves the possibility of general language and avoids absurd proliferation of distinct 'attributes' for each instance.
